source.title: Energy-Based Transformers are Scalable Learners and Thinkers
source.authors: Alexi Gladstone; Ganesh Nanduru; Md. Mofijul Islam; Peixuan Han; Hyeonjeong Ha; Aman Chadha; Yi-Lun Du; Heng Ji; Jun-Dong Li; Tariq Iqbal

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures training-loss scaling across model and training axes and compares the trends of EBTs with Transformer++ models. It uses a different experimental question and analysis from fitting and testing the original scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports scaling sweeps for language and video models, and a table comparing pretraining and downstream perplexity. These are included below. Claims about other studies' scaling laws are cited background and are not recorded as results. The paper's projected performance at much larger scales is an extrapolation, not a measurement on those larger runs. Individual plotted points are not separately extracted; each figure-level row records the described sweep.
record.test_reason: The paper trains its own small language models (Transformer++ and EBT, about 6M–400M non-embedding parameters) and video models. It reports how pretraining loss changes with data, parameters and FLOPs, and compares pretraining perplexity with downstream perplexity. That puts the claim in a new architecture setting. It fits no power laws or exponents, so the support is qualitative and figure-based.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors conclude that EBTs scale up to 35% faster than Transformer++ in pretraining across data, batch size, parameters, FLOPs, depth and width, for both text and video. They also say EBTs beat Transformer++ on 3 of 4 downstream perplexity sets despite slightly worse pretraining perplexity. Their claims of better performance at foundation scale are extrapolations: models above about 800M parameters and runs above 10^21 FLOPs were not tested.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares EBT and Transformer++ loss trends across sweeps; it does not fit and validate the original studies' scaling laws or compute-optimal allocation recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper says scaling-law findings can be sensitive to hyperparameters and data, citing a survey. In its own experiments it uses different settings across sweeps; EBT video training uses a learning rate lower by a factor of 3 for stability, and FLOP costs depend on EBT optimization steps and gradient handling. It does not systematically compare alternative fits.

fits_no_version.finding: Architecture changes the scaling rate. EBT's loss-vs-scale slope is up to about 35% steeper than Transformer++ on data, parameters, FLOPs, depth and width, with a higher intercept.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling exponents depend on architecture or training objective, not only on parameters, data and compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss falls with depth-only, width-only and batch-size sweeps for both models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-factor architecture sweeps (depth, width, batch) show monotone loss improvement.

record.problems: The authors state that models were not trained beyond 800M parameters and that training and thinking above 10^21 FLOPs were untested due to resource limits. Scaling figures do not provide fitted exponents or uncertainty estimates in the text. FLOP calculations are described as approximate. Downstream comparison uses one model pair and four datasets.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately reported numeric results bearing on the claim were left out. The paper's image-denoising and inference-time compute comparisons do not measure pretraining power-law scaling or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.

untested.parts: The power-law form, the exponents, ranges beyond about two orders of magnitude, and the non-bottleneck condition (the data sweep uses xxs models).
Not tested. Projections to Llama3 scale (Fig. B.1b, Sec. 4.1.1) are extrapolations never checked against real large runs.
Not tested. There is no fixed-compute allocation sweep.
Not tested. Depth and width are varied without holding parameter count fixed.
The fitted power-law form for video; images, fine-tuning and transfer.
Downstream scaling across model sizes. Only one model pair of the same size is compared.
No comparison of fitting methods or setups. Fragility remarks cite a survey.

missing.what: Larger-scale FineWeb data scaling (small models, batch 256, context 1024, 500k steps). EBT still out-scales Transformer++ by up to 35%; loss falls with data.
S1 vs S2 EBT scaling comparison. Same or higher slope with a higher intercept, showing training-recipe dependence of the scaling curve.
Authors' statement that the shown video axes were chosen because they behaved most linearly; other axes are unreported.

record.verdict_notes: The scaling-law claim is used mainly as a yardstick to compare architectures, so the V1 and V5 support is qualitative and figure-based: no exponents and no uncertainty. The batch-size, depth-only and width-only rows were relinked to none. The V6 rows were re-stated as reversed or observed relative to the pretraining-loss ordering.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports loss trends across several axes, but does not give fitted power-law exponents or establish the stated non-bottleneck conditions.
The paper projects results to larger scales but does not test small-run predictions against actual runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute-budget sweep identifies loss-minimising parameter and token allocations.
No controlled comparison varies depth, width, or other architecture details while holding parameter count fixed.

Video pretraining scaling is reported, but the paper does not establish that the same fitted power-law form holds across modalities. Image experiments report denoising and inference-compute comparisons, not image pretraining power-law fits. Repeated text data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested as scaling-law settings.
The paper compares one reported model pair on four downstream datasets; it does not establish a downstream scaling curve across model sizes.
The paper does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations across fitting methods or setup choices. Its remarks about fragility cite prior work.

relationships.condition: Transformer++ and EBT LMs, about 6M–400M parameters, RedPajamaV2, 105k steps
relationships.reason: The text and figures show loss falling steadily with parameters, FLOPs and data (r1, r2, r7–r10). The form is not quantified, so the support is qualitative only.
relationships.display_finding: Loss decreased steadily with parameters, FLOPs and data, although the functional form was unquantified.

relationships.condition: Autoregressive video next-frame prediction on SSV2 (repeated data), width axis
relationships.reason: Minimum validation loss falls with width for both models, and the authors say this axis behaved most linearly (r13, r14). No fit is given.
relationships.display_finding: Minimum validation loss decreased with width for both models, and the authors described width scaling as the most linear axis without reporting a fitted law.

relationships.condition: Video, non-embedding parameter axis, and other unreported video axes
relationships.reason: Authors say parameter scaling is less linear than width scaling, and they chose to show only the 'most linear' axes (r15, r16; text, Sec. 4.2).
relationships.display_finding: Non-embedding parameter scaling was less linear than width scaling, and the authors selected the most linear axes for presentation.

relationships.condition: Predicting downstream perplexity from pretraining perplexity across architectures (EBT vs Transformer++, same setup)
relationships.reason: The model with worse pretraining perplexity does better on 3 of 4 downstream sets (r19, r20, r23–r26); only SQuAD follows the ordering (r21, r22).
relationships.display_finding: The model with worse pretraining perplexity performed better on three of four downstream datasets, with only SQuAD preserving the ordering.
